chapter: Louis Jordan, Ink Spots and the union
title: Louis Jordan's band and its influence
summary: Bunn describes Jordan's Philadelphia group (Mobley, Rice, Gray, Dottie Smith), the rhythm and blues feel, and says they only played one-nighters and never recorded.

bands.name: Louis Jordan and His Tympany Five

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: So we're talking about Louis Jordan now.
Yeah. He was out of Philadelphia. I mean -- you know.
The group was out of Philadelphia. Jimmy Mobley, bass. Charlie Rice, drummer. And me, and -- oh, boy.
Then Louis Jordan. And there was a woman singer, right?

Well, about -- you know, the music itself, a lot of people give Louis Jordan credit for being the father, really, of both what got to be called rhythm and blues and then rock and roll, in a way. The stuff that the Louis Jordan bands were doing in the '40s.
It really created the style, in a way.
I mean he had the strongest single influence.
Yeah, he did. Because Louis -- I mean, Louis would get out there and do his thing, and I mean he'd do it.
What did he want out of the rhythm section? What was he looking for?
I mean, can you tell a little bit more about that, like, how was it different, say, playing with Louis Jourdan, than it was different playing, say, with Lionel Hampton?
Well, Louis had a different feeling.
See, because he was at the Cotton Club a long time by himself, with the little group he had, you know.
He had his own band. And when I joined him I joined him in Philadelphia.
Did somebody drop out of the band?
Yeah. And we went to New York. Boy. Oh, boy, boy, boy, boy.
Well, it's not exactly where -- the music itself is what's important, you know, because I don't think -- I don't think they ever recorded with you, did they?
Yeah. I don't think there's any records, Louis Jourdan records, with you on them.
No. We only done one nighters.
Yeah. You didn't have time to record.
I wonder if anybody made any --
I don't know. They might have.
Can you remember what it was like?
What was that feel? Can you like -- can you sing? Like what were the bass lines like? What was the -- how did you fit in?
Yeah. Because he didn't have a piano, did he?
He didn't have a piano, did he?
Well, I mean what do you think made the sound, what made his sound distinctive?
Yeah, his alto approach. And then he sang too, you know.
And he'd sing some pretty beautiful tunes. He was a wonderful guy. Too bad he had to pass. He was making it.
